claims.text: The first digit of a response's three-digit status code names its class; RFC 9110 defines five classes and this lesson covers the four that carry a final answer: 2xx successful, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. The fifth, 1xx, is interim.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15 Status Codes, opening list of the five classes; §15.2 (1xx Informational, interim)

claims.text: A client that receives a status code it does not recognise must not fail; it treats the answer as equivalent to the x00 code of that class.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15, paragraph on unrecognized status codes and the x00 equivalence

claims.text: 200 means the request succeeded; for a GET the representation asked for is in the body.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.3.1 200 OK (content depends on the request method)

claims.text: 201 means one or more resources were created; a POST that created resources is expected (SHOULD) to answer 201, so the method sent shapes which codes make sense.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 201 Created; §9.3.3 POST (SHOULD send 201 when resources were created)

claims.text: 204 means the request succeeded and there is deliberately no body in the response.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.3.5 204 No Content

claims.text: 301 says the target has moved permanently and 302 says the move is temporary; in both cases the server is expected (SHOULD) to name the other address in a Location header.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.4.2 301 Moved Permanently and §15.4.3 302 Found (SHOULD generate Location)

claims.text: 304 tells the client that the copy it already holds is still usable, and the response carries no body; a client may keep an earlier answer and ask whether it is still current.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.4.5 304 Not Modified; §13.1 conditional requests; §6.4.1 (no content)

claims.text: 400 means the server cannot or will not process the request because of something it perceives as a client error; 401 means the request lacks an identity the server accepts, and a server sending 401 must send a WWW-Authenticate header, which the stage-0 lab's /admin does not.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.1, §15.5.2 (MUST send WWW-Authenticate); examples/don-hang Caddyfile stage-0 lines 62-68

claims.text: 403 means the server understood the request and refuses it; 404 means the server has no current representation for the target address; 409 means the request clashes with the current state of the target, e.g. cancelling an already cancelled order.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.4 403 Forbidden, §15.5.5 404 Not Found, §15.5.10 409 Conflict

claims.text: 500 means the server that answered met an unexpected condition; 502 means a proxy got an invalid answer from the server it asked behind it; 503 means the server cannot handle the request at the moment.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.6.1 500, §15.6.3 502 Bad Gateway, §15.6.4 503 Service Unavailable

claims.text: The reason phrase printed after the number on an HTTP/1.1 status line, as in HTTP/1.1 302 Found, exists for a human reader; a client acts on the numeric code and may ignore the phrase.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9112 §4 Status Line (reason-phrase is a placeholder, clients SHOULD ignore it); RFC 9110 §15.1 (phrases are recommendations)

claims.text: A server that does not want to reveal that a forbidden target exists is allowed to answer 404 in place of 403.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.4 403 Forbidden, sentence permitting 404 instead

claims.text: 401 says the request carries no identity the server accepts, so sending one it accepts may change the answer; 403 says the server understood the request and refuses it, and repeating it with the same identity should not be expected to change the answer.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.2 401 Unauthorized and §15.5.4 403 Forbidden (MAY repeat with new or different credentials)

claims.text: At tag stage-0 the lab site answers /index.html 200, /redirect 302, /api/v1/orders/999 404, /admin 401, /conflict 409, /no-such-page 404, and /slow 503, configured to answer the way an overloaded server would.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0, :8080 route block (/slow: 'pretending to be overloaded'); outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/status-codes.txt

claims.text: At stage-0 the /redirect handler answers 302 with the header Location: /index.html, and a client that ignores that header gets nothing useful from the answer.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0, handle /redirect { redir * /index.html 302 }

claims.text: At stage-0 /admin answers 401 when the request carries no Cookie header and 403 when it carries Cookie: role=guest.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0, handle /admin route with @guest and @signedIn matchers

claims.text: In curl, the write-out variable %{http_code} prints the numeric status code of the response that was received.
claims.source_hint: curl manual, --write-out variable http_code; confirmed by outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/status-codes.txt

claims.text: In curl, -w sets what is printed after each request, -sS hides progress output but keeps error messages, -o /dev/null discards the body and -D - writes the header lines to standard output; grep -Ei '^(HTTP/|Location:)' keeps lines starting HTTP/ or Location:, any case.
claims.source_hint: curl manual, options --write-out, --silent, --show-error, --output, --dump-header; GNU grep manual, -E and -i

claims.text: Line 5 of scripts/http/status-codes.sh re-executes the script through lab-run.sh unless /.dockerenv exists, so the whole run happens inside the lab box.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/lab-run.sh and STAGE.md at stage-0, lab box paragraph

claims.text: The responder chooses the status code and nothing in HTTP derives it from the body, so a server can answer 200 with an error message in the body, contradicting what 200 means. Opinion: read the code first, then check the body for anything that contradicts it.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15 (the status code describes the result of the request) and §15.3.1 200 OK

claims.text: With only the site stopped, curl cannot connect: it reports the failed connection, the loop prints 000  /index.html (curl's placeholder, not a status code), and set -euo pipefail ends the run there. With the whole lab down, the script fails before curl runs.
claims.source_hint: curl manual, --write-out http_code (000 when no response) and exit code 7; Bash manual, set -e; scripts/lab-run.sh, scripts/down.sh at stage-0

claims.text: When a proxy answers 502, the program behind it is the first thing to look at, because 502 describes an answer the proxy got from it and could not use; a 503 may come from the proxy itself, when it is too busy or told to turn requests away.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.6.3 (gateway received an invalid response) and §15.6.4 (503 needs no intermediary)

claims.text: A 404 is a completed exchange in which the server answered, which is a different outcome from a server that is down and produces no response at all.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5.5 404 Not Found; contrast with transport failure, RFC 9110 §3.3 Connections

claims.text: 4xx: the request itself seems to be at fault, so the fix usually starts on the client's side.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.5 Client Error 4xx (class meaning); §15.5.5 (404 may be temporary)

claims.text: A 3xx answer does not carry what was asked for, but not every 3xx names another address: 301 and 302 usually point elsewhere with Location, while 304 tells the client the copy it already holds is still good.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.4 Redirection 3xx (the class), §15.4.2, §15.4.3, §15.4.5

beyond_scope: Section 4 states the rule that an unrecognised code is treated as the x00 of its class; it is not an outline item, but it makes 'the first digit is the contract' true rather than a slogan.
Section 3 uses 'reason phrase' as a plain word (not a glossary term) because outline item 4 cannot be stated without it; 'proxy' is now this lesson's vocab (owner, 2026-09-27).

Outline item 4 is only half established: 502 as written, but the lesson deliberately contradicts the outline's claim that a 503 from a proxy points at what is behind it (RFC 9110 §15.6.4 needs no intermediary, and the lab's own 503 comes from Caddy with nothing behind it).
